newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany wise men see 2.5 pct 97 growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany wise men see 2.5 pct 97 growth.

text.p: Germany's economy will grow by 2.5 percent next year while unemployment remains high and inflation benign, the Bild newspaper said on Thursday, quoting a report by a government panel of five independent economic advisers.
Bild released extracts of a report to be presented on Friday by the panel -- the so-called "wise men" -- which sees 1997 unemployment averaging 4.1 million and inflation at 1.75 percent.
A spokesman at the Economics Ministry declined to confirm the Bild report, saying only that it would be officially released on Friday.

The growth forecast was in line with the view published recently by six leading research institutes, and joins a broad consensus among economists that the recovery will gather pace after the economy expands by around one percent this year.

The panel also forecast that the total public sector budget deficit would be 114 billion marks. Bild did not say what the deficit would be when expressed as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP).

The newspaper Handelsblatt also quoted the wise men's report as saying Germany's budget deficit will miss Maastricht targets next year, falling only to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product from 4.2 percent this year.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel is aiming to cut the German budget deficit below three percent of GDP targeted by the Maastricht Treaty to qualify for EU economic and monetary union.

The institutes had predicted that the deficit would hit 3.5 percent, but Waigel has since agreed three billion marks in extra spending cuts with ministers in Germany's centre-right coalition government to try and hit his deficit goal.

Parliament's budget committee reviewed the final draft of the budget on Thursday but few changes were expected. Coalition parties were trying to squeeze the federal deficit, which does not include states and local governments, below 56 billion marks from a goal declared earlier of 56.5 billion marks.
Waigel will meet next week with state and local government leaders to thrash out final spending plans, and only then will it become clear how high the total public sector deficit will be.
Parliament will hold its second and third readings of the budget bill in two weeks.
